summary: SPACE UNIT X is a browser-based 3D learning game that helps beginners explore mission planning and orbital mechanics through interactive experiments. Players choose an Earth, Moon, or Mars scenario, prepare a spacecraft, perform orbital maneuvers, and track trajectory, velocity, fuel, and mission objectives. The project addresses the challenge of understanding how orbit, timing, and spacecraft capabilities work together by letting players see the consequences of their decisions rather than relying only on theory. It also includes a separate orbital laboratory for experiments, using NASA/JPL Horizons DE441 lunar-position data for supported dates within 2025–2026 and educational orbital models that can be compared. The project matters because it makes spaceflight concepts more approachable for students and encourages learning through experimentation and feedback. The campaign is a simplified educational simulation, not an operational navigation tool or a realistic launch-physics simulator.
details:
SPACE UNIT X is a browser-based 3D learning game designed to help students and beginners explore mission planning and orbital mechanics through experimentation. Players select from nine Earth, Moon, and Mars scenarios, prepare a spacecraft and its upgrades, then follow a simulated mission and plan maneuvers while monitoring trajectory, velocity, altitude, fuel, communications, and mission objectives. The campaign uses a simplified educational orbital model and impulsive maneuvers. Its countdown and ascent are cinematic, not a realistic physics simulation of launch.

The project was inspired by our goal of making spaceflight and orbital concepts easier to explore, as well as by mission-design references and orbital-visualization tools. It includes a separate orbital laboratory for experiments using NASA/JPL Horizons DE441 lunar-position data for supported dates within 2025–2026 and for comparing educational orbital models. This data supports the laboratory; it does not make every campaign orbit a real-date simulation. NASA GMAT/OpenFrames examples were visual references only. The project does not run GMAT and is not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.

The application was built with React, TypeScript, and Vite. Three.js renders the 3D scenes, while JavaScript modules handle orbital calculations and flight state. Browser storage retains selected progress and settings, and optional sounds are generated with the Web Audio API. No physical spacecraft hardware was used; the project runs in a web browser. Replit Agent assisted with code, interface development, debugging, testing, and documentation.

The creative aspect is the combination of a mission game with a separate science laboratory, while showing how fuel, maneuvers, and spacecraft condition affect outcomes. The team considered beginner accessibility, clear objectives and warnings, repeatable experiments, learning from failure, and the need to distinguish scientific data from illustrative models. The project aims to make orbital mechanics more interactive; its educational impact has not yet been measured in a learner study.
